title: Plan your exam preparation

blocks.title: Raj makes a decision
blocks.context: Raj has just finished the B1 checks. He talks it over with Lucie, his tutor.

lines.en: That's it, I've finished level B1! Now I'd like to take the exam, but I don't know which one to choose.

lines.fr: D'abord, vérifie ce que ton programme d'immigration demande, et quel niveau. C'est le plus important.

lines.speaker: Raj
lines.fr: Pour Entrée express, je vise le NCLC 7 dans les quatre compétences. Les deux examens sont acceptés.
lines.en: For Express Entry, I'm aiming for NCLC 7 in all four abilities. Both exams are accepted.

lines.speaker: Lucie
lines.fr: Alors, compare les épreuves. Au TEF, à l'oral, tu dois convaincre un ami. Au TCF, tu parles de toi, tu poses des questions, puis tu donnes ton opinion.
lines.en: Then compare the tests. In the TEF speaking, you have to convince a friend. In the TCF, you talk about yourself, ask questions, then give your opinion.

lines.speaker: Raj

lines.en: I quite like arguing… But in writing, I prefer shorter texts.

lines.speaker: Lucie
lines.fr: Fais un essai des deux dans le Laboratoire d'examen, et regarde où tu as les meilleurs résultats. Ensuite, on prépare un plan semaine par semaine.
lines.en: Try both in the Exam Lab and see where you get the best results. Then we'll make a week-by-week plan.

blocks.body: [[NCLC]] (Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadiens) is the French name of the Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB). [[Entrée express]] = Express Entry. [[Ça y est !]] = That's it! / Done!

blocks.title: Start with your goal, not with the exam
blocks.body:
Both **TEF Canada** and **TCF Canada** are recognised by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) and report results that convert to **NCLC levels**. The right choice depends on three questions:

1. **What does your program require?** Which tests it accepts, and which NCLC level in each ability. Rules change, so always check the official IRCC page for your program before you book.
2. **Which format suits you?** The tasks are different, especially in writing and speaking (see the table).
3. **What is practical?** Test dates, centres near you, and fees: check with the test centres in your area.

The Exam Lab gives you format-accurate practice for both exams, so the best way to decide is to **try both** and compare.

About 12 min · T1: guided interview · T2: interaction · T3: opinion

Listening and reading out of 699; writing and speaking out of 20
All four tests must be taken **on the same day**. Results valid 2 years.

blocks.title: Which exam might suit you?
head: If you…
Consider…
rows: enjoy persuading and arguing out loud
are more comfortable talking about yourself and giving a short opinion
write long texts well, and like the news-story format
prefer three shorter writing tasks with tight word ranges
TEF reading has no penalty, so guess and move on; on the TCF, bank easy points early
blocks.note: These are tendencies, not rules. Your practice results in the Exam Lab are the best evidence.

blocks.title: Before you book
blocks.body:
- **Check your program's page on the IRCC website**: accepted tests, minimum NCLC per ability, and how recent the results must be. Requirements differ between programs. For example, citizenship applicants aged 18 to 54 need at least CLB/NCLC 4 in **speaking and listening** only, while Express Entry programs score all four abilities. Check IRCC for the current rules.
- **Results must be less than two years old** for IRCC purposes (check IRCC for your program), so plan your test date around your application.
- **Register early**: popular centres fill up weeks or months ahead. Note the [[date limite]] for registration.
- Practice estimates in FrenchQuest are **unofficial and approximate**; they never predict an official result.

steps.title: Set a target and build your plan

blocks.title: NCLC: one level per ability
blocks.body:
Your official result is converted to an **NCLC level for each ability separately** (the IRCC tables for these tests run from NCLC 4 to NCLC 10): listening, reading, writing and speaking. Many programs require a minimum in **every** ability, so a weak ability can block you even if the others are strong.

As a **rough** guide only (this is not an official correspondence), B1 is around NCLC 5–6, and NCLC 7 is roughly the beginning of B2. This is why Units B2 01–12 continue your preparation.

To set your target:

1. Find the minimum your program requires.
2. Aim **one level higher** if you can, for safety and for extra points where your program awards them.
3. Save it in the Exam Lab under **My target**. The NCLC table there highlights your target row.

blocks.title: Your weekly cycle
blocks.pattern: diagnostic → pratique ciblée → série chronométrée → analyse des erreurs → production avec modèle
blocks.note:
1. **Diagnose:** do one set per ability in the Exam Lab to see where you stand.
2. **Focused practice** on your weakest ability: untimed sets with explanations after every answer.
3. **Timed set** once a week: the real time pressure, audio played once, no feedback until the end.
4. **Analyse your errors:** the results screen shows **your biggest opportunities**, the micro-skills where you lose most points (main idea, numbers, intention, paraphrase…).
5. **Write or speak** one exam task a week and compare with the models.

Keep your daily review in FrenchQuest too: vocabulary and grammar are the base of every score.

blocks.title: A sample weekly plan (about 45 minutes a day)
head: Day
Main task
In the app
rows: Listening: focused practice on your weakest micro-skill
Writing: one task in exam timing
Reading: focused practice, then review the explanations
Speaking: record one task, compare with the models
One timed set in your weakest ability
Real-life French: a podcast, the news, a conversation
Rest, or a light review; check your progress
blocks.note: **Phases:** first weeks mainly focused practice; then more timed sets; in the last two to four weeks, full mocks in exam order (all four abilities on one day, like the real TEF day). Adjust the plan to your time: 20 minutes a day, every day, beats three hours once a week.

blocks.title: Words to talk about your preparation
Preparation mistakes
blocks.body:
- **Only practising your strong ability.** It feels good, but the weakest ability decides whether you reach your target.
- **Never practising under time.** Many candidates know the answers but run out of time. From B1, do at least one timed set a week.
- **Booking too early or too late.** Book when your timed practice is at or near your target, and leave time for a second attempt before your application deadline.
- **Ignoring writing and speaking** because they are harder to practise alone. Record yourself, use the checklists, and compare with the models.
- **Saying [[J'ai passé le TEF]] to mean “I passed the TEF”.** It means “I took it”. To pass = [[réussir]].

steps.title: Check your plan
steps.intro: Quick questions on choosing and preparing.

blocks.prompt: Which exam has three writing tasks with word ranges of 60–120, 120–150 and 120–180 words?
blocks.explain: TCF writing has tasks T1, T2 and T3. TEF writing has two sections: A (80–120 words) and B (200–250 words).

blocks.prompt: In which exam must all four tests be taken on the same day for the certificate to be recognised?
blocks.explain: This is a TEF Canada rule. Plan for a long day and practise full mocks in exam order.

blocks.prompt: Your program requires NCLC 7 in each ability. Your practice estimates are NCLC 8 in reading, 8 in writing, 7 in speaking and 6 in listening. What should you focus on?
blocks.explain: NCLC is checked ability by ability: listening is below the minimum, so it is your priority. Keep the others alive with lighter practice.

blocks.prompt: What do the practice estimates in the Exam Lab tell you?
options: An approximate, unofficial idea of where you stand
blocks.explain: Estimates help you track progress, but they never predict an official result. Only the real test counts.

blocks.prompt: Match the French and the English.

Write your preparation plan in French (80–150 words), as if you were explaining it to your tutor. Say which exam you choose and why, your NCLC target, your strong and weak points, and what you will do each week. Then open the Exam Lab, choose your exam and save your target.
blocks.promptFr: Présentez votre plan de préparation : l'examen choisi, votre objectif, vos points forts et faibles, et votre programme de la semaine.
checklist: The exam you choose and at least one reason (parce que, comme…)
One strong point and one weak point
What you will do each week, with days or times
A date: when you plan to take the exam
At least one futur simple (je ferai, je passerai…)
Optional: si + imparfait → conditionnel (Si j'avais plus de temps, je…)

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: J'ai décidé de passer le TCF Canada, parce que je préfère les textes courts à l'écrit. Mon objectif est le NCLC 7 dans les quatre compétences, pour Entrée express. Mon point fort, c'est la lecture. Mon point faible, c'est la compréhension orale : je ne comprends pas toujours les chiffres. Chaque semaine, je ferai trois séances d'écoute de 30 minutes, une tâche écrite et une tâche orale. Le vendredi, je ferai une série chronométrée. Je passerai l'examen en juin.
models.en: I've decided to take the TCF Canada, because I prefer short texts in writing. My target is NCLC 7 in all four abilities, for Express Entry. My strong point is reading. My weak point is listening: I don't always understand numbers. Every week, I'll do three 30-minute listening sessions, one writing task and one speaking task. On Fridays, I'll do a timed set. I'll take the exam in June.

models.label: Stronger model answer
models.fr: Après avoir essayé les deux examens dans le Laboratoire d'examen, j'ai choisi le TEF Canada. J'aime argumenter, et j'ai eu de meilleurs résultats à la tâche où il faut convaincre un ami. Mon programme demande le NCLC 7, mais je vise le NCLC 8 en lecture et en écriture, mes points forts, pour avoir une marge de sécurité. En revanche, l'oral reste mon point faible : je parle encore trop lentement. C'est pourquoi je m'entraînerai à l'expression orale trois fois par semaine, en m'enregistrant. Le mardi et le jeudi, je ferai une série d'écoute, et chaque dimanche, une tâche écrite chronométrée. Si tout se passe bien, je ferai un examen blanc complet début mai, et je passerai le vrai examen à la fin juin.
models.en: After trying both exams in the Exam Lab, I chose the TEF Canada. I like arguing, and I got better results on the task where you have to convince a friend. My program requires NCLC 7, but I'm aiming for NCLC 8 in reading and writing, my strong points, to have a safety margin. On the other hand, speaking is still my weak point: I still speak too slowly. That's why I'll practise speaking three times a week, recording myself. On Tuesdays and Thursdays, I'll do a listening set, and every Sunday, a timed writing task. If all goes well, I'll do a full mock exam at the beginning of May, and I'll take the real exam at the end of June.

summary:
- Compare TEF Canada and TCF Canada task by task, and check your program's requirements on the IRCC website
- Set an NCLC target for each ability, and save it in the Exam Lab
- Follow a weekly cycle: diagnose, focused practice, timed sets, error analysis, writing and speaking with models
- Talk about your preparation: [[passer]] vs [[réussir un examen]], [[point faible]], [[s'entraîner]], [[examen blanc]]
